children.title: Nonconvex Descent Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Objective or model decrease behavior in nonconvex composite regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Descent Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic descent for smooth nonconvex plus convex nonsmooth composite objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=f+g\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(f\) is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and may be nonconvex, while \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex. For a constant \(0<\alpha<2/L\), define
\[
x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha g}(x_k-\alpha\nabla f(x_k)).
\]
Then every finite-valued iterate satisfies
\[
F(x_{k+1})\le F(x_k)-\left(\frac1\alpha-\frac L2\right)\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|^2.
\]
Consequently, if \(F\) is bounded below along the iterates, then \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|^2<\infty\) and \(\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a stepsize below twice the reciprocal smoothness constant, proximal gradient decreases the composite objective and has square-summable successive displacements.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(F(x_0)<+\infty\).
\(0<\alpha<2/L\), and \(F\) is bounded below along the iterates for the summability conclusion.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the gradient of f.

children.title: Subsequence Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Stationarity guarantees attached to convergent subsequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Subsequence Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing proximal-gradient residual and existence of an approximately stationary subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the assumptions of deterministic nonconvex proximal-gradient descent, define
\[
G_\alpha(x)=\frac1\alpha\left(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha g}(x-\alpha\nabla f(x))\right).
\]
If \(F\) is bounded below and \(0<\alpha<2/L\), then the descent inequality yields
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|G_\alpha(x_k)\|^2<\infty,
\qquad \|G_\alpha(x_k)\|\to0.
\]
Hence there exists a subsequence \((x_{k_j})\) whose stationarity residual converges to zero. If that subsequence converges to \(\bar x\), then closedness of the convex subdifferential graph and continuity of \(\nabla f\) imply \(0\in\nabla f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Descent makes the proximal-gradient residual vanish; every convergent subsequence therefore approaches a composite stationary point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(0<\alpha<2/L\), and \(F=f+g\) is bounded below along the iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|G_\alpha(x_k)\|\to0\), and any stated subsequential limit satisfies \(0\in\nabla f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\).

children.title: Limit-Point Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Stationarity properties of accumulation points.

knowledge_statements.title: Limit-Point Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity of every accumulation point of a bounded proximal-gradient sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((x_k)\) be generated by proximal gradient for \(F=f+g\), where \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, \(F\) is bounded below along the iterates, and \(0<\alpha<2/L\). Then \(\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0\). For any accumulation point \(\bar x\), choose \(x_{k_j}\to\bar x\); the vanishing displacement also gives \(x_{k_j+1}\to\bar x\). The proximal optimality condition
\[
0\in\partial g(x_{k_j+1})+\nabla f(x_{k_j})+\frac1\alpha(x_{k_j+1}-x_{k_j})
\]
therefore passes to the limit, so every accumulation point satisfies \(0\in\nabla f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every accumulation point of a descent-generating proximal-gradient sequence is composite stationary; boundedness guarantees that at least one such point exists.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(0<\alpha<2/L\), and \(F=f+g\) is bounded below along the iterates.
An accumulation point exists; boundedness of the sequence is sufficient.

notation.meaning: Set of subsequential limits of the iterate sequence.
An accumulation point of the iterates.

children.title: Descent Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where standard descent interpretations cease to apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Descent Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp stepsize failure on a smooth quadratic, already within the proximal-gradient family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The restriction \(\alpha<2/L\) cannot be removed even when the nonsmooth term vanishes. Let \(f(x)=\tfrac L2x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), let \(g=0\), and choose \(x_0\ne0\). Proximal gradient becomes
\[
x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha L)x_k,
\qquad f(x_{k+1})=(1-\alpha L)^2f(x_k).
\]
At \(\alpha=2/L\), the iterates alternate between \(x_0\) and \(-x_0\), so neither displacement nor stationarity residual vanishes. For \(\alpha>2/L\), one has \(|1-\alpha L|>1\), and both \(|x_k|\) and \(f(x_k)\) grow geometrically. Thus global descent fails at and beyond the threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a scalar quadratic, stepsize two over the smoothness constant causes oscillation, and any larger stepsize makes the objective grow geometrically.

notation.meaning: Quadratic curvature and gradient Lipschitz constant.

children.title: Nonconvex Stationarity Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Stationarity Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic proximal-gradient complexity measured by the squared proximal-gradient mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=f+g\), where \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(F_{\inf}=\inf_xF(x)>-\infty\). Run proximal gradient with \(\alpha=1/L\), and define \(G_{1/L}(x)=L\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{g/L}(x-\nabla f(x)/L)\bigr)\). For every integer \(K\ge1\),
\[
\min_{0\le k<K}\|G_{1/L}(x_k)\|^2
\le \frac{2L\bigl(F(x_0)-F_{\inf}\bigr)}{K}.
\]
Thus finding an iterate with \(\|G_{1/L}(x_k)\|\le\varepsilon\) requires at most \(\left\lceil2L(F(x_0)-F_{\inf})/\varepsilon^2\right\rceil\) proximal-gradient oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basic proximal gradient reaches an iterate with stationarity residual at most epsilon in order epsilon to the minus two gradient-plus-proximal oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex.
Each iteration uses one gradient evaluation and one proximal evaluation with stepsize \(1/L\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonconvex proximal-gradient residual bound and convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded guarantee for proximal-gradient iterates using either the constant or backtracking stepsize rule in the theorem's nonconvex setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{\mathbf{x}_k\}\) be generated by the proximal-gradient method in the nonconvex setting using either a constant or a backtracking stepsize rule, and define \(\gamma_n:=\min_{1\le k\le n}\|\mathbf{x}_{k-1}-p_{L_k}(\mathbf{x}_{k-1})\|\). For every \(n\ge1\), \[\gamma_n\le \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\left(\frac{2\bigl(F(\mathbf{x}_0)-F_*\bigr)}{\beta L(f)}\right)^{1/2}.\] Moreover, \(\|\mathbf{x}_{k-1}-p_{L_k}(\mathbf{x}_{k-1})\|\to0\) as \(k\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the theorem's nonconvex setting, proximal-gradient iterates generated with either the constant or backtracking stepsize rule have a best-iterate residual bounded by the stated constant times 1/sqrt(n), while the full residual sequence converges to zero.
assumptions_latex: The problem is in the nonconvex setting of Theorem 2.3.

children.title: Convex Objective Complexity
children.top_down_role: Objective-value convergence for basic proximal-gradient methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Objective Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-gap rate for basic constant-stepsize proximal gradient in the convex case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=f+g\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(f\) is convex and differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, and a minimizer \(x^\star\) exists. Starting from \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}g\), run
\[
x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{g/L}\left(x_k-\frac1L\nabla f(x_k)\right).
\]
Then for every integer \(k\ge1\),
\[
F(x_k)-F(x^\star)\le\frac{L\|x_0-x^\star\|^2}{2k}.
\]
Consequently, an objective gap at most \(\varepsilon>0\) is obtained after at most \(\left\lceil L\|x_0-x^\star\|^2/(2\varepsilon)\right\rceil\) gradient-plus-proximal oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex composite objective, basic proximal gradient has an objective gap of order one over iterations and needs order one over epsilon oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x_k)-F(x^\star)\le L\|x_0-x^\star\|^2/(2k)\), hence the oracle complexity is \(O(\varepsilon^{-1})\).

notation.meaning: A minimizer of the composite objective.

children.title: Accelerated Convex Objective Complexity
children.top_down_role: Improved convex objective convergence for FISTA-type families.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Convex Objective Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical constant-step FISTA objective bound for convex composite minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+g\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(f\) is convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}F\). Initialize \(x_0=y_1\), \(t_1=1\), and, for \(k\geq1\), set \(x_k=\operatorname{prox}_{g/L}(y_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(y_k))\), \(t_{k+1}=(1+\sqrt{1+4t_k^2})/2\), and \(y_{k+1}=x_k+((t_k-1)/t_{k+1})(x_k-x_{k-1})\). Then \[F(x_k)-F(x^*)\leq \frac{2L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2}{(k+1)^2}.\] Consequently, an objective error at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(O(\!\sqrt{L}\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert/\sqrt{\varepsilon}\!)\) gradient and proximal evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: FISTA decreases convex composite objective error as inverse iteration squared, reaching accuracy epsilon in order square-root inverse-epsilon gradient and proximal evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
\(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(\operatorname*{argmin}F\neq\varnothing\).
The step size is \(1/L\) and the displayed FISTA momentum sequence is used.

notation.meaning: Proximal mapping of the scaled nonsmooth term.

However, no inspectable citation is supplied for the exact indexing, constant, and oracle-complexity conclusion, so the record remains source-dependent.

children.title: Strongly Convex Linear-Convergence Regime
children.top_down_role: Geometric convergence for strongly convex composite objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Linear-Convergence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-value linear rate for constant-step proximal gradient under strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+g\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(f\) is convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(0<\mu\leq L\). For the proximal-gradient iteration \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{g/L}(x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k))\), the unique minimizer \(x^*\) satisfies \[F(x_k)-F(x^*)\leq \left(1-\frac{\mu}{L}\right)^k\bigl(F(x_0)-F(x^*)\bigr).\] Hence \(O((L/\mu)\log((F(x_0)-F^*)/\varepsilon))\) gradient and proximal evaluations suffice to obtain objective error at most \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity changes proximal-gradient objective convergence from sublinear to geometric, with iteration complexity proportional to the condition number times a logarithmic accuracy factor.
assumptions_latex: \(F=f+g\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and the step size is \(1/L\).

notation.meaning: Strong-convexity modulus of the composite objective.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric objective-gap bound for V-FISTA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded condition-number-dependent convergence guarantee for V-FISTA on the referenced strongly convex composite problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\{x^k\}_{k\geq0}\) be generated by V-FISTA for minimizing \(F\), and let \(\kappa=L_f/\sigma\). Then, for every \(x^*\in X^*\) and every integer \(k\geq0\),
\[
F(x^k)-F_{\mathrm{opt}}
\leq
\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\right)^k
\left(F(x^0)-F_{\mathrm{opt}}+\frac{\sigma}{2}\lVert x^0-x^*\rVert^2\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If Assumption 10.31 holds and f is sigma-strongly convex, the V-FISTA objective gap is at most the initial objective-and-distance error multiplied by (1-1/sqrt(kappa))^k, where kappa=L_f/sigma.
assumptions_latex: \(\{x^k\}_{k\geq0}\) is generated by V-FISTA for the composite minimization problem.

children.title: Error-Bound-Quadratic-Growth Regularity Classes

children.title: Error-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Linear-rate settings organized through error-bound geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local proximal-gradient residual error bound around the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+g\), let \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}F\neq\varnothing\), and fix \(\alpha>0\). Define the proximal-gradient mapping by \[G_\alpha(x)=\alpha^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha g}(x-\alpha\nabla f(x))\bigr).\] A local proximal-gradient error bound holds on a set \(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}F\) if there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq\kappa\lVert G_\alpha(x)\rVert\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] A sublevel-local regime takes \(U=\{x:F(x)\leq F^*+\delta\}\cap B(X^*,r)\) for some \(\delta,r>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An error-bound regime controls distance to the solution set by the norm of the proximal-gradient residual, either locally or on a specified sublevel neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on a neighborhood of \(U\).
\(g\) is proper and closed, and the displayed proximal mapping is nonempty on \(U\).

notation.meaning: Proximal-gradient mapping at step size alpha.
Neighborhood or sublevel region on which the bound holds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the terminal, but the displayed proximal-gradient mapping is written as single-valued while g is assumed only proper and closed rather than convex or otherwise prox-regular with a selected mapping. A source is needed to fix the intended regime and its hypotheses.

children.title: Quadratic-Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Linear-rate settings organized through objective growth near solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Growth Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local or global quadratic objective growth away from the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and let \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}F\neq\varnothing\), with minimum value \(F^*\). The function has quadratic growth with modulus \(\mu_q>0\) on \(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}F\) if \[F(x)-F^*\geq\frac{\mu_q}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,X^*)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] The regime is global when \(U=\operatorname{dom}F\), and local when \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(X^*\) or a sufficiently small objective sublevel set. Quadratic growth does not require the minimizer to be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth lower-bounds objective error by a positive multiple of squared distance to the entire solution set, either globally or in a declared neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper and attains its finite minimum \(F^*\).

notation.meaning: Set of minimizers of the objective.
Region on which quadratic growth is asserted.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind and set-valued quadratic-growth formulation match the terminal and are mathematically standard. Nevertheless, the record supplies no inspectable source with a definition, section, theorem, or page locator.

children.title: Regularity Equivalences
children.top_down_role: Relationships among fast-rate regularity conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity Equivalences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative convex equivalence between quadratic growth and subdifferential metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(x^*\in X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}F\). The following local properties are equivalent, with possibly different neighborhoods and positive constants: \[F(x)-F^*\geq\frac{\mu_q}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,X^*)\] for all feasible \(x\) near \(x^*\); and metric subregularity of the convex subdifferential at \((x^*,0)\), namely \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\] for all feasible \(x\) near \(x^*\). Uniform constants over the solution set are additionally required for a uniform neighborhood statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed convex objectives, local quadratic growth is equivalent to local metric subregularity of the subdifferential, subject to matching local and uniformity conventions.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
Both properties use local neighborhoods and allow their constants to differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local quadratic growth at \(x^*\) is equivalent to metric subregularity of \(\partial F\) at \((x^*,0)\).

notation.meaning: Zero set of the subdifferential and minimizer set.
Positive regularity constants, not asserted to be reciprocal.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind is appropriate, but the precise equivalence depends on pointwise versus uniform quadratic growth, neighborhood conventions, and the form of metric subregularity. It also concerns a subdifferential error bound rather than the proximal-gradient residual bound in the cited prerequisite node. An exact theorem source is required.

children.title: Locality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinction between neighborhood regularity and global regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Locality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local regularity yields no global rate before iterates enter its validity region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic-growth or error-bound inequality asserted only on \(U\) cannot by itself imply a global linear rate from arbitrary initialization; a convergence argument must first show that the iterates enter and remain in \(U\). The convex smooth function \(F(x)=x^4\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) illustrates the sharp boundary at its minimizer \(0\): neither \[x^4\geq\frac{\mu}{2}|x|^2\] nor \[|x|\leq\kappa|F'(x)|=4\kappa|x|^3\] holds on any neighborhood of \(0\) for positive \(\mu\) or finite \(\kappa\). Fixed-step gradient descent consequently has no local geometric contraction factor bounded strictly below one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local regularity gives a linear rate only after neighborhood entry. The convex function x-to-the-fourth lacks both quadratic growth and a gradient error bound near zero.
assumptions_latex: A claimed regularity inequality is available only on a specified set \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local assumptions do not imply a global rate, and \(F(x)=x^4\) admits no positive local quadratic-growth or residual error-bound constant at \(0\).

notation.meaning: Validity region of the local regularity condition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the terminal, and the x^4 calculations are directly checkable. No source is supplied for the broader locality-to-rate boundary, including the required entry-and-invariance qualification and the stated absence of a uniform local geometric factor.

children.title: Stochastic Variance-Reduced Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Oracle-complexity families for stochastic forward–backward methods.

children.title: Stochastic Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Oracle costs for baseline stochastic forward–backward methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected objective complexity for averaged stochastic proximal subgradient iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+g\) be convex, let \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}F\), and suppose an oracle returns \(v_k\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[v_k\mid x_k]\in\partial f(x_k)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert v_k\rVert^2\mid x_k]\leq G^2\). Assume \(\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert\leq R\). For \(K\geq1\), use \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta g}(x_k-\eta v_k)\), \(\eta=R/(G\sqrt K)\), and \(\bar x_K=K^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}x_k\). Then \[\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_K)-F^*]\leq\frac{RG}{\sqrt K}.\] Thus at most \(\lceil R^2G^2/\varepsilon^2\rceil\) stochastic oracle calls suffice for expected objective error at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaged stochastic proximal iterations achieve expected convex objective error of order one over square-root iterations, hence require order inverse-epsilon-squared oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: \(F=f+g\) is convex and attains its minimum.
The stochastic subgradient oracle is conditionally unbiased with second moment at most \(G^2\).
The initial distance to a minimizer is at most \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_K)-F^*]\leq RG/\sqrt K\), giving oracle complexity \(O(R^2G^2/\varepsilon^2)\).

notation.meaning: Stochastic subgradient returned at iteration k.
Average of the first K iterates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits the terminal, but convexity of F alone does not establish the convex subgradient and proximal inequalities used by the displayed method; the intended assumptions normally require suitable convexity of f and g. A theorem source is also needed for the exact averaging and constant.

children.title: Variance-Reduced Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Oracle costs for variance-reduced proximal-gradient methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Reduced Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strongly convex finite-sum proximal SVRG component-gradient complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)+g(x)\), where every \(f_i\) is convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex. A proximal SVRG scheme using periodic full-gradient snapshots, a sufficiently small constant step, and an epoch length proportional to \(L/\mu\) produces an output \(\widetilde x_s\) satisfying \[\mathbb{E}[F(\widetilde x_s)-F^*]\leq\rho^s(F(\widetilde x_0)-F^*)\] for some \(\rho\in(0,1)\). Counting individual component-gradient evaluations, expected error at most \(\varepsilon\) is attained with \[O\!\left(\left(n+\frac{L}{\mu}\right)\log\frac{F(\widetilde x_0)-F^*}{\varepsilon}\right)\] evaluations and the same order of proximal steps up to epoch accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal SVRG removes the persistent stochastic variance and reaches strongly convex finite-sum accuracy with component-gradient cost proportional to n plus the condition number, times a logarithm.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
Proximal SVRG uses admissible fixed step and epoch-length parameters.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind and strongly convex finite-sum placement are appropriate. The claim depends on a particular proximal-SVRG variant, snapshot-output rule, step size, epoch length, and accounting convention, none of which is tied to an inspectable theorem locator.

children.title: Finite-Sum Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity organization for finite-sum composite objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Complexity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-cost comparison between full-gradient and variance-reduced finite-sum regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)+g(x)\), one exact proximal-gradient iteration evaluates all \(n\) component gradients. If the \(f_i\) are convex and \(L\)-smooth and \(\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert\leq R\), accelerated full-gradient proximal iterations therefore use \[O\!\left(n\sqrt{\frac{LR^2}{\varepsilon}}\right)\] component-gradient evaluations to reach objective error \(\varepsilon\). If \(F\) is additionally \(\mu\)-strongly convex, a standard proximal variance-reduced method instead uses \[O\!\left(\left(n+\frac{L}{\mu}\right)\log\frac{F(x_0)-F^*}{\varepsilon}\right)\] component-gradient evaluations. These bounds use different convexity regimes and are not interchangeable without their stated assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-sum cost depends on whether full gradients or variance reduction are used and whether mere convexity or strong convexity supplies the convergence regime.
assumptions_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i+g\), with convex \(L\)-smooth components and proximable closed convex \(g\).
The first bound assumes \(\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert\leq R\).
The second bound additionally assumes \(\mu\)-strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full-gradient acceleration costs \(O(n\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\), while strong-convexity variance reduction costs \(O((n+L/\mu)\log((F(x_0)-F^*)/\varepsilon))\).

notation.meaning: Finite-sum size and cost of one full gradient.
Initial distance bound for the convex regime.
Condition number in the strongly convex regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits this comparison terminal, and the two regimes are explicitly distinguished. Sources are still required for both bounds, especially to verify whether L denotes each component's smoothness or an aggregate smoothness constant and which variance-reduced algorithm supports the second complexity.

children.title: Noise-Floor Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Accuracy limitations caused by persistent stochastic noise.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Floor Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-step stochastic gradients generally converge only to a variance-dependent neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the smooth special case \(g=0\) and stochastic gradient descent \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta(\nabla f(x_k)+\xi_k)\), where \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth, \(\mathbb{E}[\xi_k\mid x_k]=0\), and \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert\xi_k\rVert^2\mid x_k]\leq\sigma^2\). For a standard admissible constant step \(0<\eta\leq1/L\), the mean-square recursion yields a geometric transient plus a residual of order \(\eta\sigma^2/\mu\): \[\mathbb{E}\lVert x_k-x^*\rVert^2\leq(1-\mu\eta)^k\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2+O\!\left(\frac{\eta\sigma^2}{\mu}\right).\] Thus fixed nonzero variance and fixed step size preclude arbitrarily accurate convergence; decreasing steps, increasing batches, or variance reduction is required to remove the floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a fixed step and persistent gradient variance, stochastic descent retains a variance-dependent error floor; vanishing steps, growing batches, or variance reduction are needed for arbitrary accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The noise is conditionally unbiased with conditional second moment at most \(\sigma^2\).
The step size is constant and satisfies \(0<\eta\leq1/L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic mean-square error is generally \(O(\eta\sigma^2/\mu)\), rather than zero.

notation.meaning: Fixed step size controlling the noise floor.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind is appropriate. The displayed upper recursion gives a possible residual scale but, under only an upper bound on noise variance, does not itself prove that convergence to zero is precluded; a persistent-noise assumption or an explicit lower-bound example is needed. A source must also verify the contraction and residual constants.

children.title: Active-Manifold Identification Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Structural identification and subsequent local convergence regimes.

children.title: Active-Manifold Identification
children.top_down_role: Recognition of active local structure by proximal-gradient iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Manifold Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite identification under partial smoothness and strict complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+g\), where \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable near a critical point \(x^*\), and \(g\) is proper, closed, convex, and partly smooth at \(x^*\) relative to a \(C^2\) manifold \(\mathcal M\). Suppose proximal-gradient iterates with step sizes bounded inside \((0,2/L)\) converge to \(x^*\), and the nondegeneracy condition \[-\nabla f(x^*)\in\operatorname{ri}\partial g(x^*)\] holds. Then the iterates identify the active manifold in finite time: there exists \(K<\infty\) such that \[x_k\in\mathcal M\qquad\text{for every }k\geq K.\] The conclusion concerns manifold membership, not finite convergence to \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial smoothness, convergence, and strict complementarity imply that proximal-gradient iterates enter the active manifold after finitely many iterations and never leave it locally.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is convex and partly smooth at \(x^*\) relative to a \(C^2\) manifold \(\mathcal M\).
The proximal-gradient iterates converge to \(x^*\) with admissible step sizes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(K<\infty\) such that \(x_k\in\mathcal M\) for all \(k\geq K\).

notation.meaning: Active manifold relative to which the regularizer is partly smooth.
Relative interior of the convex subdifferential.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind precisely matches the active-identification terminal. However, the phrase 'bounded inside (0,2/L)' is not a complete variable-step condition, and finite-identification results can require additional continuity or parameter assumptions. An exact partial-smoothness theorem locator is required.

children.title: Post-Identification Local Behavior
children.top_down_role: Local convergence behavior after active structure is identified.

knowledge_statements.title: Post-Identification Local Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local smooth-manifold dynamics and restricted-curvature rates after finite identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the hypotheses of finite active-manifold identification, so that \(x_k\in\mathcal M\) for all \(k\geq K\). If the restrictions of \(f\) and \(g\) to \(\mathcal M\) are twice continuously differentiable near \(x^*\), then the subsequent proximal-gradient dynamics admit a smooth local linearization on the tangent space \(T_{\mathcal M}(x^*)\). If the Riemannian Hessian of \(F|_{\mathcal M}\) at \(x^*\) is positive definite and the fixed step is locally admissible, the linearized iteration has spectral radius \(\rho<1\), and \[\lVert x_{k+1}-x^*\rVert\leq(\rho+o(1))\lVert x_k-x^*\rVert.\] Thus the eventual local rate is governed by curvature restricted to the identified manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After identification, proximal gradient behaves as a smooth iteration on the active manifold; positive restricted curvature gives a local linear rate governed by the tangent-space linearization.
assumptions_latex: The iterates finitely identify \(\mathcal M\) and converge to \(x^*\).
The objective restricted to \(\mathcal M\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(x^*\).
The restricted Riemannian Hessian is positive definite and the step is locally admissible.

notation.meaning: Tangent space of the identified manifold at the limit.
Restriction of the objective to the active manifold.
Spectral radius of the local tangent-space linearization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind is acceptable for the terminal, but positive restricted curvature and a vaguely 'locally admissible' step do not by themselves document the precise proximal-gradient Jacobian or guarantee its spectral radius is below one. The algorithm-specific linearization and rate require an authoritative theorem source.

children.title: Identification Stability
children.top_down_role: Persistence of identified structure under local perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Identification Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite identification under partial smoothness, nondegeneracy, and vanishing computational perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+g\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose \(x_k\to x_\star\), where \(g\) is partly smooth at \(x_\star\) relative to a manifold \(\mathcal M\). Consider perturbed forward-backward steps \[x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma_k g}\!\left(x_k-\gamma_k(\nabla f(x_k)+e_k)\right)+r_k.\] If \(0<\underline\gamma\leq\gamma_k\leq\overline\gamma\), \(e_k\to0\), \(r_k\to0\), the iterates satisfy the required proximal residual consistency, and \(-\nabla f(x_\star)\in\operatorname{ri}\partial g(x_\star)\), then there exists \(K\) such that \(x_k\in\mathcal M\) for all \(k\geq K\). The conclusion persists under sufficiently small perturbations that preserve convergence, residual consistency, and the relative-interior condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent perturbed forward-backward sequence eventually remains on the active manifold when partial smoothness, residual consistency, and strict nondegeneracy hold.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable near \(x_\star\), and \(g\) is proper and partly smooth there relative to \(\mathcal M\).
\(x_k\to x_\star\), \(e_k\to0\), \(r_k\to0\), and the proximal residuals are consistent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists K\;\forall k\geq K:\ x_k\in\mathcal M\), stably under perturbations preserving the hypotheses.

notation.meaning: active manifold of the partly smooth regularizer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Vanishing additive output perturbations r_k do not generally preserve exact finite manifold identification: arbitrarily small nonzero r_k can keep x_{k+1} outside the manifold forever. The undefined residual-consistency hypothesis does not repair this overstatement, and no source is supplied.

children.title: Degeneracy Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where finite or stable identification can fail.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite support identification when relative-interior nondegeneracy is replaced by boundary inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\lambda>0\) and minimize \(F(x)=f(x)+g(x)\) on \(\mathbb R\), where \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^2-\lambda x\) and \(g(x)=\lambda|x|\). The unique minimizer is \(x_\star=0\), but \(-f'(0)=\lambda\in\partial g(0)=[-\lambda,\lambda]\) lies on the boundary rather than in its relative interior. For any \(0<\gamma<1\) and \(x_0>0\), proximal gradient gives \[x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}\!\left(x_k-\gamma f'(x_k)\right)=(1-\gamma)x_k.\] Hence \(x_k\downarrow0\) while \(x_k>0\) for every finite \(k\); the active manifold \(\{0\}\) is never identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a degenerate solution, proximal-gradient iterates may converge to the solution without ever identifying its active manifold.

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the absolute-value regularizer at zero

children.title: Stepsize-Majorization Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of descent or stability under unsuitable curvature estimates.

children.title: Stepsize Failure
children.top_down_role: Instability or progress loss caused by unsuitable stepsizes.

knowledge_statements.title: Stepsize Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp constant-stepsize failure on a one-dimensional smooth quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac{L}{2}x^2\) with \(L>0\) and let \(g\equiv0\). Proximal gradient with constant stepsize \(\gamma>0\) reduces to \[x_{k+1}=(1-\gamma L)x_k.\] If \(0<\gamma<2/L\), every initial point converges to zero. If \(\gamma=2/L\) and \(x_0\neq0\), then \(x_k=(-1)^k x_0\), so the iterates do not converge and the objective is constant. If \(\gamma>2/L\), then \(|x_k|=|1-\gamma L|^k|x_0|\to\infty\). Thus the usual smooth convex convergence range cannot be extended beyond \(2/L\) for unrestricted constant-step proximal gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a quadratic, the threshold 2/L is sharp: equality causes a two-cycle, and larger steps make the iterates diverge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma=2/L\) yields a nonconvergent two-cycle, while \(\gamma>2/L\) yields divergence.

notation.meaning: gradient Lipschitz constant and quadratic curvature

children.title: Majorization Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of model validity when local curvature is underestimated.

knowledge_statements.title: Majorization Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at which the forward-backward quadratic surrogate ceases to majorize the smooth term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and define the proximal-gradient surrogate at \(x\) by \[Q_\gamma(z;x)=f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),z-x\rangle+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|z-x\|^2+g(z).\] The descent lemma guarantees \(F(z)\leq Q_\gamma(z;x)\) for every \(x,z\) whenever \(\gamma\leq1/L\). For \(\gamma>1/L\), uniform majorization is impossible over this function class: with \(g\equiv0\), \(f(z)=\tfrac{L}{2}\|z\|^2\), and \(x=0\), one has \(f(z)-Q_\gamma(z;0)=\tfrac12(L-1/\gamma)\|z\|^2>0\) for every \(z\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard proximal-gradient surrogate majorizes every L-smooth objective exactly up to stepsize 1/L; beyond it, a quadratic violates majorization.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(g\) is proper with a well-defined surrogate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform majorization holds for \(\gamma\leq1/L\) and fails in general for \(\gamma>1/L\).

knowledge_statements.title: Descent-Loss Regimes

Let \(F=f+g\), where \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex. For \(x^+=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma

eq x\). At \(\gamma=2/L\) the guaranteed decrease coefficient vanishes. For \(\gamma>2/L\), descent fails in general: taking \(g\equiv0\) and \(f(x)=	frac L2x^2\) gives \(F(x^+)>F(x)\) for every \(x

children.title: Curvature-Misestimation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity to inaccurate curvature information.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Misestimation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of replacing the true smoothness constant by an underestimated curvature model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, and the algorithm uses a curvature estimate \(M>0\) with \(\gamma=1/M\). For the proximal-gradient update \(x^+\), \[F(x^+)\leq F(x)-\left(M-\frac L2\right)\|x^+-x\|^2.\] Hence \(M>L/2\) guarantees strict descent, whereas the stronger surrogate-majorization property requires \(M\geq L\). If \(M<L/2\), the quadratic instance \(f(x)=\tfrac L2x^2\), \(g\equiv0\), satisfies \(F(x^+)>F(x)\) for every \(x\neq0\). At \(M=L/2\), the same instance produces equal objective values and alternating iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Underestimating curvature below L loses majorization; below L/2 it can also make a proximal-gradient step increase the objective.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The selected stepsize is \(\gamma=1/M\) for an estimate \(M>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Majorization needs \(M\geq L\); uniform strict descent needs \(M>L/2\).

children.title: Acceleration Instability
children.top_down_role: Unstable behavior caused by inertial extrapolation.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceleration Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral stability boundary for a constant-inertia accelerated step on a quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac L2x^2\), \(g\equiv0\), and apply the constant-inertia scheme \[y_k=x_k+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=y_k-\gamma Ly_k.\] Writing \(a=1-\gamma L\), the iterates satisfy \(x_{k+1}=a(1+\beta)x_k-a\beta x_{k-1}\). Its characteristic polynomial is \(p(r)=r^2-a(1+\beta)r+a\beta\). The zero solution is asymptotically stable exactly when both roots of \(p\) have modulus strictly below one. If the spectral radius is greater than one, some initial pair produces geometrically growing iterates; if it equals one, convergence is not guaranteed. Thus acceleration stability depends jointly on stepsize and inertia.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a quadratic inertial iteration, convergence holds exactly when both recurrence roots lie inside the unit disk; crossing that boundary causes instability.

notation.meaning: characteristic polynomial of the inertial recurrence

children.title: Objective Nonmonotonicity
children.top_down_role: Temporary or persistent objective increases under acceleration.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Nonmonotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-step increase caused by inertial extrapolation despite a conservative forward stepsize.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac L2x^2\), \(g\equiv0\), choose \(\gamma=1/(2L)\), and use \(y_k=x_k+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1})\), \(x_{k+1}=y_k-\gamma\nabla f(y_k)\). With \(0<\beta<1\), \(x_{-1}=1\), and \(x_0=0\), one obtains \[y_0=-\beta,\qquad x_1=-\frac\beta2.\] Consequently \(F(x_0)=0\) but \(F(x_1)=L\beta^2/8>0\). Thus an accelerated proximal-gradient step need not generate a monotone objective sequence even though the underlying noninertial stepsize lies safely below \(2/L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Momentum can increase the objective in one step even when the corresponding noninertial gradient stepsize is safely convergent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x_1)>F(x_0)\), so inertial objective values are not necessarily monotone.

children.title: Oscillatory Iterate Behavior
children.top_down_role: Iterate oscillation near solutions or across active structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Oscillatory Iterate Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oscillation criterion for quadratic inertial proximal-gradient dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac L2x^2\), \(g\equiv0\), constant \(\gamma\), and constant inertia \(\beta\), set \(a=1-\gamma L\). The inertial recurrence has characteristic polynomial \[p(r)=r^2-a(1+\beta)r+a\beta.\] If \(a\beta>0\) and \(a^2(1+\beta)^2-4a\beta<0\), its roots are a nonreal conjugate pair. Every nonzero real trajectory is then a damped, persistent, or expanding oscillation according as \(\sqrt{a\beta}<1\), \(\sqrt{a\beta}=1\), or \(\sqrt{a\beta}>1\). Thus iterate oscillation can occur even within the convergent regime, where its envelope decays but successive errors rotate in the two-dimensional recurrence state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complex recurrence roots produce oscillatory inertial iterates; their common modulus determines whether the oscillation decays, persists, or grows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A negative discriminant yields oscillation, with envelope ratio \(\sqrt{a\beta}\).

notation.meaning: modulus of each conjugate characteristic root

children.title: Restart-Relevant Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavioral regimes motivating acceleration restarts.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart-Relevant Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable objective-based condition for suppressing an unproductive inertial extrapolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an inertial proximal-gradient iteration \[y_k=x_k+\beta_k(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma_k g}\!\left(y_k-\gamma_k\nabla f(y_k)\right),\] the objective-restart condition at iteration \(k\) is \[F(x_{k+1})>F(x_k).\] When this predicate holds and both objective values are finite, the extrapolated trial has lost monotonic descent relative to the accepted iterate. An objective restart discards that trial momentum by setting \(\beta_k=0\), recomputing the step from \(x_k\), and restarting the momentum schedule. The condition is a computable trigger, not by itself a claim that every restarted scheme converges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective increase is a directly checkable restart trigger: discard the inertial trial, recompute without momentum, and reset the schedule.

children.title: Accumulated Oracle Error
children.top_down_role: Convergence and rate degradation under uncontrolled forward or proximal errors.

knowledge_statements.title: Accumulated Oracle Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence boundary created by nonsummable additive errors in an otherwise exact fixed-point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an inexact forward-backward update written as \[x_{k+1}=T(x_k)+e_k,\qquad T=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}\circ(I-\gamma\nabla f).\] Summability conditions such as \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|e_k\|<\infty\) prevent unbounded accumulated displacement in standard quasi-Fejér analyses. Without any control on accumulated error, convergence can fail even for a trivial objective: take \(f\equiv g\equiv0\), so \(T=I\), and choose \(e_k=1/(k+1)\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(x_k=x_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e_j\to+\infty\), although every point is stationary for the exact problem and \(e_k\to0\). Vanishing error alone therefore does not ensure iterate convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Errors may vanish individually yet accumulate without bound; summability-type control is needed in standard inexact convergence analyses.
assumptions_latex: The inexact iteration has additive errors \(e_k\).
No summability or cancellation condition is imposed on \((e_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condition \(e_k\to0\) alone does not imply convergence of \((x_k)\).

notation.meaning: aggregate oracle or proximal error at iteration \(k\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The harmonic-error counterexample correctly shows that e_k tending to zero is insufficient, but the broader claim about summability in standard inexact forward-backward and quasi-Fejer analyses has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Stationarity without Global Optimality
children.top_down_role: The solution-quality boundary of nonconvex proximal-gradient certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity without Global Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A zero proximal-gradient mapping at a nonglobal stationary point of a smooth nonconvex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=1-\cos x\) on \(\mathbb R\) and \(g\equiv0\). The gradient \(f'(x)=\sin x\) is globally \(1\)-Lipschitz. For any \(\gamma>0\), define the proximal-gradient mapping \[G_\gamma(x)=\frac1\gamma\left(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma f'(x))\right).\] At \(x=\pi\), one has \(G_\gamma(\pi)=0\), so the standard proximal-gradient stationarity certificate is exact. Nevertheless, \(F(\pi)=2\), whereas \(F(0)=0\), and therefore \(\pi\) is not globally optimal. In a nonconvex composite problem, a small or zero gradient mapping certifies stationarity, not global solution quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero proximal-gradient mapping can occur at a nonglobal point; nonconvex stationarity certificates do not certify global optimality.

children.title: Convex-Composite Models

children.title: Pure Convex-Composite Models
children.top_down_role: The core nonlinear composition class underlying prox-linear methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Pure Convex-Composite Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-outer, smooth-inner model without an additional regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(c:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable and let \(h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex. A pure convex-composite problem is
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} F(x),\qquad F(x):=h(c(x)).
\]
The adjective convex-composite refers to convexity of the outer function \(h\); the objective \(F\) need not be convex because \(c\) may be nonlinear. At a base point \(x\), its convex linearized model is
\[
m_x(z):=h\bigl(c(x)+\nabla c(x)(z-x)\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pure convex-composite objective applies a proper closed convex function to a smooth, possibly nonlinear mapping; consequently, the resulting objective can be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=h\circ c\), with convex linearized model \(m_x(z)=h(c(x)+\nabla c(x)(z-x))\).

notation.meaning: convex composite model obtained by linearizing the inner mapping at x

children.title: Regularized Convex-Composite Models
children.top_down_role: Convex-composite objectives augmented by a simple extended-valued component.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Convex-Composite Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-composite objective with a proximable extended-valued regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(c:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex. A regularized convex-composite problem has the form
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} F(x),\qquad F(x):=h(c(x))+g(x).
\]
The extended values of \(g\) may encode a convex constraint set. The associated convex model at \(x\) is
\[
m_x(z):=h\bigl(c(x)+\nabla c(x)(z-x)\bigr)+g(z).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularized model adds a proper closed convex term, possibly encoding constraints, to a convex outer function composed with a smooth nonlinear mapping.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=h(c(x))+g(x)\), and linearizing \(c\) produces the convex model \(m_x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard regularized convex-composite model underlying prox-linear methods
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Nonlinear Least-Squares Specialization
children.top_down_role: The specialization linking prox-linear and Gauss–Newton methodology.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Least-Squares Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least-squares convex-composite model and its regularized Gauss–Newton subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a continuously differentiable residual mapping \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), nonlinear least squares is the convex-composite problem
\[
F(x)=\frac12\lVert r(x)\rVert^2=h(r(x)),\qquad h(u)=\frac12\lVert u\rVert^2.
\]
Given \(t>0\), the prox-linear subproblem at \(x\) is
\[
x^+\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^n}
\left\{\frac12\left\lVert r(x)+\nabla r(x)(z-x)\right\rVert^2+\frac{1}{2t}\lVert z-x\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
Thus the prox-linear step is precisely a quadratically regularized Gauss–Newton step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For squared residual loss, linearizing the residual map yields the Gauss–Newton quadratic model; adding the proximal quadratic gives a regularized Gauss–Newton step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The prox-linear subproblem for \(h(u)=\tfrac12\lVert u\rVert^2\) is the regularized Gauss–Newton subproblem.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct specialization of the convex-composite model to squared Euclidean loss
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation correctly identifies the regularized Gauss–Newton specialization, but no prox-linear or Gauss–Newton source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Exact-Penalty Composite Models
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth composite penalty models arising from constrained optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Penalty Composite Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth convex-composite penalties for smooth equality and inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider smooth constraint mappings \(a:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(b:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^q\), with desired constraints \(a(x)=0\) and \(b(x)\leq 0\). For \(\rho>0\), the violation penalty admits the convex-composite representation
\[
P_\rho(x)=\rho h(c(x)),\qquad c(x):=(a(x),b(x)),
\]
where
\[
h(u,v):=\lVert u\rVert_1+\sum_{i=1}^{q}\max\{v_i,0\}.
\]
The function \(h\) is finite and convex, and \(P_\rho(x)=0\) exactly when all displayed constraints hold. Whether a local minimizer of a penalized objective is also constrained-optimal requires an appropriate exact-penalty threshold and constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality violations measured by an l1 norm and positive inequality violations form a convex outer penalty composed with the smooth constraint mapping.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard l1 and hinge exact-penalty composite representation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Regularized Linearized Composite Model
children.top_down_role: The local convex model defining prox-linear methodology.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Linearized Composite Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strongly convex local model defining one prox-linear trial point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=h(c(x))+g(x)\), a base point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\), and \(t>0\), define the regularized linearized composite model
\[
Q_t(z;x):=h\bigl(c(x)+\nabla c(x)(z-x)\bigr)+g(z)+\frac{1}{2t}\lVert z-x\rVert^2.
\]
Its minimizer set defines the prox-linear update
\[
T_t(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^n}Q_t(z;x).
\]
Because the first two terms are convex in \(z\) and the final term is \(1/t\)-strongly convex, \(T_t(x)\) contains at most one point; it is a singleton whenever the minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The prox-linear model linearizes the smooth inner mapping, retains both convex terms exactly, and adds a quadratic that makes the subproblem strongly convex.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex, and \(c\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever attained, \(T_t(x)\) is the unique minimizer of \(Q_t(\cdot;x)\).

children.title: Prox-Linear Gradient Mapping
children.top_down_role: The principal displacement-based certificate for prox-linear steps.

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Linear Gradient Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Displacement certificate associated with an exact Euclidean prox-linear step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the regularized model \(Q_t(\cdot;x)\) has the unique minimizer \(x^+=T_t(x)\). The prox-linear gradient mapping is
\[
G_t(x):=\frac{1}{t}\bigl(x-T_t(x)\bigr).
\]
It is directly computable from the accepted model step and satisfies \(\lVert G_t(x)\rVert=\lVert x-x^+\rVert/t\). Moreover, \(G_t(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\) minimizes its own linearized model. Under the convex-composite subdifferential chain rule, this fixed-point condition is equivalent to
\[
0\in \nabla c(x)^{\mathsf T}\partial h(c(x))+\partial g(x),
\]
which is first-order composite stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The prox-linear gradient mapping rescales the displacement to the exact model minimizer; its vanishing certifies a model fixed point and, under the chain rule, composite stationarity.
assumptions_latex: The convex-composite subdifferential chain rule holds at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_t(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in\nabla c(x)^{\mathsf T}\partial h(c(x))+\partial g(x)\).

notation.meaning: exact minimizer of the regularized linearized model

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical displacement-based prox-linear stationarity measure
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displacement certificate fits the container, but the asserted equivalence with composite stationarity depends on a precisely specified subdifferential and chain/sum-rule qualification that lacks source support.

children.title: Composite Model Residual
children.top_down_role: Stationarity certification derived from the local convex model.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Model Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality residual for exact or inexact solutions of the convex prox-linear subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a base point \(x\), parameter \(t>0\), and trial point \(z\in\operatorname{dom}g\), define the composite model residual
\[
r_t(x;z):=\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla c(x)^{\mathsf T}\partial h\bigl(c(x)+\nabla c(x)(z-x)\bigr)+\partial g(z)+\frac{1}{t}(z-x)\right).
\]
Whenever the displayed convex subdifferential sum rule is valid, this equals \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_z Q_t(z;x))\). Hence \(r_t(x;z)=0\) if and only if \(z=T_t(x)\). An inexact model solution satisfying \(r_t(x;z)\leq\varepsilon\) therefore carries a verifiable \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate for the strongly convex local subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model residual measures violation of the linearized subproblem’s optimality inclusion; zero residual identifies the exact prox-linear step, while a small residual certifies inexact solution quality.
assumptions_latex: The convex subdifferential chain and sum rules apply to \(Q_t(\cdot;x)\).

notation.meaning: distance from the origin to a set S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subdifferential residual is the standard computable optimality certificate for a convex model subproblem
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual is a suitable certificate, but the phrase “epsilon-optimality certificate” does not specify whether epsilon measures residual, distance, or objective gap. The required calculus qualifications and interpretation need an authoritative locator.

children.title: Envelope-Based Composite Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Moreau-envelope interpretation of prox-linear progress and termination.

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope-Based Composite Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau-envelope gradient as a stationarity measure for a weakly convex composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex. For \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\), define
\[
F_\lambda(x):=\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{F(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\},
\qquad
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{F(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
The envelope is continuously differentiable and
\[
\nabla F_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(x)\bigr).
\]
Thus \(\lVert\nabla F_\lambda(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) is an envelope-based stationarity certificate, and zero gradient is equivalent to \(x\in\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a weakly convex composite objective, the Moreau-envelope gradient is a scaled proximal displacement; its norm supplies a smooth stationarity measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla F_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(x))\), so its norm certifies envelope stationarity.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical differentiability formula for the Moreau envelope of a weakly convex function
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weakly convex Moreau-envelope certificate is standard and fits the leaf, but no source with a section, theorem, or page locator is provided.

children.title: Prox-Linear Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: The classical prox-linear method and its adaptive, inexact, and stochastic extensions.

children.title: Basic Prox-Linear Method
children.top_down_role: The foundational regularized convex-linearization method.

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Prox-Linear Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fixed-parameter prox-linear iteration for regularized convex-composite minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}g\), a parameter \(t>0\), and a termination tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\). For \(k=0,1,2,\ldots\), compute
\[
x_{k+1}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^n}
\left\{h\bigl(c(x_k)+\nabla c(x_k)(z-x_k)\bigr)+g(z)+\frac{1}{2t}\lVert z-x_k\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
Define \(G_t(x_k):=t^{-1}(x_k-x_{k+1})\). Stop and output \(x_k\) when \(\lVert G_t(x_k)\rVert\leq\varepsilon\); otherwise continue from \(x_{k+1}\). The iteration is well-defined whenever every displayed strongly convex subproblem attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, linearize the smooth inner map, retain the convex terms, add a fixed proximal quadratic, solve exactly, and stop when the scaled displacement is small.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex, while \(c\) is continuously differentiable.
Each model subproblem attains its minimum.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical exact fixed-stepsize prox-linear iteration
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and fixed-parameter prox-linear iteration fit the leaf, but the algorithm has no cited prox-linear source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Adaptive Prox-Linear Calibration Methods
children.top_down_role: Prox-linear families with adaptive regularization and model acceptance.

children.title: Adaptive Prox-Linear Regularization
children.top_down_role: Prox-linear methods adapting local regularization strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Prox-Linear Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ratio-based adjustment of the quadratic regularization strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}g\), \(M_0>0\), thresholds \(0<\eta_1\leq\eta_2<1\), and factors \(\gamma_+>1\), \(0<\gamma_-<1\). At iteration \(k\), compute
\[
z_k:=\operatorname*{argmin}_z\left\{m_{x_k}(z)+\frac{M_k}{2}\lVert z-x_k\rVert^2\right\},
\]
then set the predicted and actual reductions to \(\Delta_k^{\rm pred}:=F(x_k)-m_{x_k}(z_k)\) and \(\Delta_k^{\rm act}:=F(x_k)-F(z_k)\). If \(\Delta_k^{\rm pred}>0\), form \(\rho_k:=\Delta_k^{\rm act}/\Delta_k^{\rm pred}\). Accept \(z_k\) when \(\rho_k\geq\eta_1\). Increase \(M_k\) after rejection, decrease it when \(\rho_k\geq\eta_2\), and otherwise retain it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare actual and model-predicted decrease, accept sufficiently accurate trials, strengthen quadratic regularization after rejection, and weaken it after very successful trials.
assumptions_latex: Every regularized model subproblem has a minimizer.
The ratio is evaluated only when \(\Delta_k^{\rm pred}>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Set \(x_{k+1}=z_k\) if \(\rho_k\geq\eta_1\), otherwise \(x_{k+1}=x_k\), with \(M_{k+1}\in\{\gamma_-M_k,M_k,\gamma_+M_k\}\) selected by the acceptance regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Ratio definitions and regularization updates vary across adaptive prox-linear methods. No source supports this particular predicted reduction, acceptance rule, or update convention.

children.title: Prox-Linear Line Search
children.top_down_role: Prox-linear methods using trial acceptance through line search.

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Linear Line Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backtracking along a prox-linear direction using sufficient objective decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\), \(t>0\), \(\sigma\in(0,1)\), and \(\beta\in(0,1)\). Compute the full prox-linear trial \(z=T_t(x)\) and direction \(d=z-x\). Starting with \(\alpha=1\), test
\[
F(x+\alpha d)\leq F(x)-\frac{\sigma\alpha}{2t}\lVert d\rVert^2.
\]
If the test fails, replace \(\alpha\) by \(\beta\alpha\) and repeat. On the first successful test, output \(x^+=x+\alpha d\). If \(d=0\), terminate at \(x\) with a zero prox-linear gradient mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute a prox-linear direction, backtrack geometrically until a sufficient-decrease inequality holds, then accept the damped trial; a zero direction terminates the method.
assumptions_latex: The objective is finite at every tested trial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted point is \(x^+=x+\beta^j d\) for the first \(j\geq0\) satisfying the sufficient-decrease test.

children.title: Model-Acceptance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Acceptance interfaces based on local model quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Acceptance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-way classification based on actual-to-predicted model reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be a current point, \(z\) a model trial, and suppose
\[
\Delta^{\rm pred}:=F(x)-m_x(z)>0,
\qquad
\rho:=\frac{F(x)-F(z)}{\Delta^{\rm pred}}.
\]
For fixed thresholds \(0<\eta_1\leq\eta_2<1\), classify the trial as unsuccessful when \(\rho<\eta_1\), successful when \(\eta_1\leq\rho<\eta_2\), and very successful when \(\rho\geq\eta_2\). The corresponding acceptance condition is \(\rho\geq\eta_1\). In a ratio-based adaptive scheme, an unsuccessful trial leaves the iterate unchanged and requests stronger regularization; a very successful trial permits weaker regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ratio of actual to predicted decrease partitions trials into unsuccessful, successful, and very successful regimes and determines acceptance and regularization adjustment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accept \(z\) exactly when \(\rho\geq\eta_1\); the intervals cut by \(\eta_1\) and \(\eta_2\) define the three regimes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the acceptance-regime leaf, but the predicted-reduction definition, threshold convention, and associated regularization actions are algorithm-dependent and lack a supporting locator.

children.title: Rejection-Stagnation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failure modes caused by repeated trial rejection or ineffective adaptation.

knowledge_statements.title: Rejection-Stagnation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional backtracking boundary for deterministic prox-linear model acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi(x)=h(F(x))+g(x)\), where \(h\) is \(L_h\)-Lipschitz and \(F'\) is \(L_F\)-Lipschitz. For \(d=y-x\), define \(\widehat\Phi_x(y)=h(F(x)+F'(x)d)+g(y)\). Then \(\Phi(y)\leq \widehat\Phi_x(y)+(L_hL_F/2)\lVert d\rVert^2\). Consequently, the acceptance test \(\Phi(y)\leq\widehat\Phi_x(y)+(1/(2t))\lVert d\rVert^2\) is guaranteed whenever \(t\leq (L_hL_F)^{-1}\). A rejection loop replacing \(t\) by \(\gamma t\), with \(0<\gamma<1\), therefore terminates finitely. If rejected trials do not force \(1/t\) above the model-error curvature \(L_hL_F\), finite termination and outer progress are not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtracking cannot stagnate once regularization dominates the linearization error; without eventually crossing that curvature threshold, repeated rejection may continue indefinitely.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is convex and \(L_h\)-Lipschitz on the relevant image set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\leq(L_hL_F)^{-1}\) guarantees model acceptance; failure to reach this regime permits rejection stagnation.

notation.meaning: Unregularized prox-linear model at the current point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and threshold calculation are mathematically plausible, but no source supports the exact acceptance convention, curvature constant, or termination claim.

children.title: Inexact Prox-Linear Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods coordinating approximate convex inner solves with outer progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Prox-Linear Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic prox-linear iteration with objective-gap-controlled convex inner solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}g\), parameters \(t_k>0\), tolerances \(\varepsilon_k\geq0\), and \(\Phi(x)=h(F(x))+g(x)\), define \[Q_k(y)=h(F(x_k)+F'(x_k)(y-x_k))+g(y)+\frac{1}{2t_k}\lVert y-x_k\rVert^2.\] Compute \(x_{k+1}\) satisfying \(Q_k(x_{k+1})\leq\inf_y Q_k(y)+\varepsilon_k\). Define the inexact prox-gradient estimate \(G_k=t_k^{-1}(x_k-x_{k+1})\). Stop when a prescribed test combining \(\lVert G_k\rVert\) and \(\varepsilon_k\) is met; otherwise increment \(k\). For asymptotic outer accuracy, select the inner tolerances so that their accumulated contribution to the chosen descent analysis is finite or tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each outer iteration approximately minimizes the strongly convex prox-linear model, while a decreasing or summable inner-error policy preserves meaningful outer progress.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.
\(F\) is differentiable on a neighborhood of the iterates.
Each model has a finite minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\) is an \(\varepsilon_k\)-optimal solution of the current prox-linear subproblem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inner objective-gap update is well defined, but the claim about preserving outer progress does not specify the required weighted or unweighted error condition and has no supporting source.

children.title: Stochastic Prox-Linear Methods
children.top_down_role: Sample-based prox-linear methods for stochastic convex-composite objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Prox-Linear Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mini-batch prox-linear method using sampled values and sampled Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi(x)=h(F(x))+g(x)\), with stochastic oracles \(F(x;\xi)\) and \(J(x;\xi)\). Given \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}g\), batch sizes \(B_k\), and \(t_k>0\), draw a batch \(S_k\) and form \(\widehat F_k=B_k^{-1}\sum_{\xi\in S_k}F(x_k;\xi)\) and \(\widehat J_k=B_k^{-1}\sum_{\xi\in S_k}J(x_k;\xi)\). Compute an exact or controlled-inexact minimizer \[x_{k+1}\approx\arg\min_y\left\{h(\widehat F_k+\widehat J_k(y-x_k))+g(y)+\frac{1}{2t_k}\lVert y-x_k\rVert^2\right\}.\] Stop under a prescribed stationarity or budget test; otherwise resample and continue. Batch growth, variance reduction, or decreasing \(t_k\) must control sampling error relative to the requested outer accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampled function values and Jacobians define a random convex model whose approximate minimizer becomes the next outer iterate.
assumptions_latex: The sampled value and Jacobian estimators are measurable and have controlled bias and variance.
\(h\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.
The displayed sampled subproblem admits a minimizer almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update is obtained by minimizing a sampled regularized linearization of the convex-composite objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relationship between F(x), F(x;xi), and the sampling distribution is not defined. Consequently, the sample-average model may represent a composition of expectations, an expected composition, or a biased surrogate; a source and precise stochastic formulation are required.

children.title: Prox-Linear Inner Computation

children.title: Primal Convex Inner Solvers
children.top_down_role: Inner methods operating directly on prox-linear subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Convex Inner Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct primal solution of a regularized convex prox-linear subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an outer point \(x\), set \(A=F'(x)\), \(b=F(x)-Ax\), and \(r_x(y)=g(y)+(1/(2t))\lVert y-x\rVert^2\). The inner problem is \[\min_y P_x(y),\qquad P_x(y)=h(Ay+b)+r_x(y).\] Initialize \(y^0\), apply a convergent primal convex method using available values, subgradients, gradients, or proximal maps of the displayed terms, and terminate at the first \(j\) for which a verifiable primal criterion gives \(P_x(y^j)-\inf_yP_x(y)\leq\varepsilon\), or an equivalent certified residual bound. Return \(y^j\) as the outer trial point. The quadratic term makes \(P_x\) \(1/t\)-strongly convex whenever \(g\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal inner solver directly minimizes the strongly convex linearized composite model and returns a point meeting the requested inner tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(t>0\), and \(g\) and \(h\) are proper, closed, and convex.
The selected primal method has access to its required first-order or proximal oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned point is an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate primal solution of the prox-linear inner problem.

notation.meaning: Affine representation of the linearized mapping.

source_refs.locator: 6 The Proximal Operator p. 129

The instruction to apply an arbitrary convergent primal method is also too broad to establish the stated return guarantee.

children.title: Dual-Structured Inner Solver Family

children.title: Dual Inner Solvers
children.top_down_role: Inner convex solvers operating through dual formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Inner Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-dual solution method for the convex prox-linear inner problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(y)=h(Ay+b)+r(y)\), where \(r(y)=g(y)+(1/(2t))\lVert y-x\rVert^2\). Under Fenchel qualification, \[\inf_y P(y)=\sup_u\left\{-h^*(u)-r^*(-A^*u)+\langle b,u\rangle\right\}.\] A dual inner solver maximizes the right-hand objective to a prescribed dual or primal-dual tolerance. From a dual iterate \(u\), a corresponding primal candidate is \(y(u)=\arg\min_y\{r(y)+\langle A^*u,y\rangle\}\), equivalently \(y(u)=\nabla r^*(-A^*u)\) when \(r^*\) is differentiable. The primal-dual gap, when both objectives are finite, certifies inner accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual inner solver maximizes the Fenchel dual of the convex prox-linear subproblem and recovers a primal candidate by minimizing the regularized primal term.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) and \(r\) are proper, closed, and convex on finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong duality holds, and dual iterates admit primal recovery through \(r^*\).

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugates of h and r.

children.title: Primal–Dual Inner Solvers
children.top_down_role: Inner solvers maintaining coupled primal–dual representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Inner Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual hybrid-gradient iteration for a prox-linear inner saddle problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_y r(y)+h(Ay+b)\), use the saddle function \(L(y,u)=r(y)+\langle u,Ay+b\rangle-h^*(u)\). Choose \(\tau,\sigma>0\) with \(\tau\sigma\lVert A\rVert^2<1\), initialize \(y^0,u^0\), and set \(\bar y^0=y^0\). Iterate \[u^{j+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma h^*}\bigl(u^j+\sigma(A\bar y^j+b)\bigr),\] \[y^{j+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau r}\bigl(y^j-\tau A^*u^{j+1}\bigr),\qquad \bar y^{j+1}=y^{j+1}+\theta(y^{j+1}-y^j),\] with \(\theta\in[0,1]\). Stop when a prescribed primal-dual gap or KKT residual is at most \(\varepsilon\), and return \(y^{j+1}\) to the outer method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled proximal updates of primal and dual variables solve the inner saddle problem without explicitly eliminating either variable.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) and \(r\) are proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration targets a saddle point whose primal component solves the prox-linear inner problem.

children.title: Operator-Splitting Inner Solvers
children.top_down_role: Primal–dual inner computation organized through operator splitting.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Splitting Inner Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Douglas–Rachford splitting for a two-term convex inner objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the inner objective as \(P(y)=f(y)+r(y)\), where \(f(y)=h(Ay+b)\). Choose \(\lambda>0\), relaxation \(\rho\in(0,2)\), and initialize \(z^0\). Iterate \[y^j=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda r}(z^j),\qquad v^j=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(2y^j-z^j),\qquad z^{j+1}=z^j+\rho(v^j-y^j).\] Stop when \(\lVert v^j-y^j\rVert\) or a certified objective-gap criterion meets the requested inner tolerance, and return \(y^j\). Equivalently, this applies Douglas–Rachford splitting to the monotone inclusion \(0\in\partial f(y)+\partial r(y)\). The formulation is useful only when both displayed proximal mappings can be evaluated efficiently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas–Rachford splitting alternates the proximal maps of the affine composite term and the regularized primal term.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(r\) are proper, closed, and convex.
Both required proximal maps are computable to the intended accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed points yield primal solutions of \(\min_y f(y)+r(y)\).

children.title: Dualization Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limits on useful or tractable dual reformulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Dualization Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint qualification and computational boundaries for Fenchel dual inner formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P(y)=h(Ay+b)+r(y)\) in finite dimensions, the dual equality \[\inf_yP(y)=\sup_u\{-h^*(u)-r^*(-A^*u)+\langle b,u\rangle\}\] and dual attainment are ensured by a suitable Fenchel qualification, for example continuity of \(h\) at some point of \(A\operatorname{dom}r+b\), or the corresponding relative-interior condition. If qualification fails, a duality gap or nonattainment may occur, so a dual residual need not certify primal inner accuracy. Even under strong duality, dualization is computationally unsuitable when \(h^*\), \(r^*\), their proximal maps, or applications of \(A^*\) are unavailable or substantially harder than the primal oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual inner solution is reliable only under strong-duality qualification and useful only when conjugate, proximal, and adjoint operations are tractable.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) and \(r\) are proper, closed, and convex on finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absent qualification or tractable dual oracles, dualization cannot safely serve as the inner-solver interface.
